terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where the demo plays the dock board: next tours, then the whole day.

tasks.title: Catch the timetable changing
tasks.description:
Before you change anything, prove both halves of the bug. In `src/reproduce.js`, implement `reproduceReorder()`.

Copy `harbourTour` into a new array, then call the original `nextDepartures(copy, 600)`. Return an object with:

- `before`: the contents of your copy before the call (a second copy, so it cannot change)
- `result`: what `nextDepartures` returned
- `after`: your copy, read after the call

The check runs your function against the original `departures.js`.
nextSteps: Run `node src/demo.js` and compare the full day with `timetable.js`.
Copy `harbourTour` with the spread syntax and save a second copy as `before`.
Call `nextDepartures` with the first copy and return all three.
Run the demo again and read `after`.
hints: Two things are wrong in the demo: the order of the next tours, and the full day printed after the call.
`[...harbourTour]` makes a new array. If `before` and `after` are the same array, they will always look the same.
Return the same array you passed to `nextDepartures` as `after`. It should now start with 1020.

tasks.title: Sort by time, and leave the timetable alone
tasks.description:
Fix `nextDepartures(times, now, count = 3)` in `src/departures.js`.

- It returns at most `count` departures that are at or after `now`, earliest first, as numbers.
- `times` can be in any order and can hold small values like `75` (01:15).
- It must not change the array it is given, so it also works on a frozen array.

Keep `formatTime` as it is. The check calls `nextDepartures` with several timetables, then looks at both the result and the array it passed in.
nextSteps: Decide how two numbers should be compared and pass that to `sort`.
Make sure the array you sort is not the one the caller gave you.
Keep the filter for `now` and the `slice` for `count`.
Run `node src/demo.js` and check the full day stays in order.
hints: Without a compare function, `sort` turns each value into a string and compares the strings, so '1020' comes before '540'.
`sort` changes the array it is called on and returns that same array. `filter`, `slice` and spread all return a new one.
Sort a new array with a compare function that returns a negative number when `a` should come first, such as the difference of the two.

tasks.title: Write the test that would have caught it
tasks.description:
Write vitest tests in `src/departures.test.js` that guard both halves of this bug:

- the next departures come back in time order, for times that sort differently as text
- the array passed to `nextDepartures` is exactly the same afterwards

The check runs your test file three times: beside the original `departures.js` (it must fail), beside a correct fix (it must pass) and beside a fix that adds a numeric compare function but still sorts the caller's array in place (it must fail).
nextSteps: Import `nextDepartures` and write a test for the order of the result.
Write a second test that passes in an unsorted array and checks it afterwards.
Run `npx vitest run src/departures.test.js` against your fixed code.
Ask yourself what the in place fix still gets wrong.
hints: Use an array you own in the test, not the shared `harbourTour`, so one test cannot change another.
Keep a reference to the array you pass in, call the function, then `expect` that same array to equal the order you wrote.
The in place fix returns the right answer. Only the test that checks the input array afterwards can catch it, so the input must start out of order.
